title: "Father, Son, and Holy Spirit": How Islam Understands the Holy Spirit Differently
summary: What Islamic tradition identifies as the Holy Spirit, and why it isn't the third person of a Trinity in Islamic theology.

body.text: A familiar term, a different meaning

"Holy Spirit" (Ruh al-Qudus) appears in the Quran too, which can be genuinely confusing for a revert — the phrase sounds identical to the Christian term, but it refers to something meaningfully different in Islamic theology.
Mainstream Islamic identification: the Angel Gabriel

The dominant view among Islamic scholars identifies "the Holy Spirit" in the Quran with the Angel Jibril (Gabriel) — the same angel who delivered revelation to the Prophet Muhammad and, according to Islamic tradition, was involved in strengthening and supporting Jesus during his ministry. This is a created being, an angel, not a person of the Godhead sharing in God's own nature — a fundamentally different category than the Christian Holy Spirit.

body.translation: And We gave Jesus, the son of Mary, clear proofs and supported him with the Pure Spirit.

body.text: Why this matters for the Trinity discussion

Since Islam identifies the Holy Spirit as a created angel rather than a divine person, there's no room within Islamic theology for a "third person" of the Godhead — reinforcing the objection to the Trinity covered in an earlier lesson from a different angle. This is a good example of how Islamic and Christian theology can use overlapping vocabulary while operating on entirely different underlying frameworks, which is worth remembering broadly whenever a term sounds familiar across the two faiths.
A secondary, less common Islamic reading

A minority of scholars have read some Quranic references to "spirit" as referring more generally to a divine, life-giving force from God rather than specifically the angel Gabriel — but even this reading stops well short of describing the Holy Spirit as a distinct divine person, which is the specific Christian claim this lesson is addressing. Either way, mainstream Islamic theology treats the term very differently from its Christian counterpart.

body.question: So is the "Holy Spirit" mentioned in the Quran actually the same thing Christians mean?
body.answer: No — this is one of the clearest examples in this collection of shared vocabulary describing genuinely different concepts. The Quran's Holy Spirit is understood as a created angel (commonly identified as Gabriel), not a co-equal, co-eternal divine person as in Christian Trinitarian doctrine.

body.question: Does this mean the Holy Spirit is unimportant in Islam?
body.answer: Not at all — the angel Gabriel holds an extremely significant role in Islamic theology as the deliverer of revelation to every prophet, including the entire Quran to Muhammad. The disagreement with Christianity is specifically about whether this figure is a created being or a divine person, not about the figure's overall importance.

body.question: Did discovering that "Holy Spirit" means something different in Islam change how you'll listen for shared vocabulary between the two faiths going forward?
